parole.significato: An unleavened bread, usually made with barleymeal, wheatmeal, or oatmeal; sometimes of peasemeal or otherwise.
parole.testo: From Middle English bannoke, from Old English bannuc, perhaps from a Goidelic word (compare Irish bonnóg, Manx bonnag, Scottish Gaelic bonnach), possibly from Latin pānicum (“millet”). Doublet of bonnag.

parole.significato: One of a class of anchorites who lived in various parts of Scotland, Ireland, and Wales in the Middle Ages.
parole.testo: From Old Irish céile Dé (“servant of God”), a calque of Latin servus Deī.

parole.significato: The head of a clan occupying church lands under a bishop in Gaelic Ireland.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Irish airchinnech, from Proto-Celtic *ɸare-kʷenno- (“extremity, end”); see *kʷennom (“head”).

parole.testo: Origin unknown. Possibly from Old Irish fid

parole.significato: A member of the semi-divine race that were said to have inhabited Ireland in ancient times.
parole.testo: Probably Old Irish fo- (“under”) + mor, mur (“ocean”).

parole.significato: A Gael; a member of the Goidelic division of Celtic languages as opposed to the Brythonic division.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Old Irish Goídel (“Gael”). Doublet of Gael.

parole.significato: An Old Irish tale of a sea voyage to a mythical land.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Irish imram (“sea voyage”).

parole.significato: A fairy that supposedly appears in animal form, often large.
parole.testo: From Old Irish púca (“goblin, sprite”), perhaps from a (nearly) identical Old Irish form, ultimately from Old English pūca (“demon”). Doublet of bucca and puck.

parole.significato: To drink or imbibe with vigour or relish; to drink copiously; to swallow in large draughts.
parole.testo: Uncertain. Suggestions include connection with Old Irish cuäch (“cup, goblet, bowl; cauldron, large vessel; bowl, cup”) (whence Scots quaich, queff). The noun is derived from the verb.

parole.significato: A walled enclosure, especially in Ireland; a ringfort built sometime between the Iron Age and the Viking Age.
